oil.summary: Crude prices extended their brutal slide on July 2, with WTI settling at $67.75/bbl (-1.24% on the day, -5.83% on the week, and a staggering -27.76% on the month) as supply-side relief overwhelmed lingering geopolitical noise. Saudi Arabia rushed roughly 10 million barrels through the reopened Strait of Hormuz via Ras Tanura, while Chinese teapot refiners opportunistically snapped up discounted Middle Eastern spot cargoes. Iran continued to complicate the picture: Tehran is demanding approved routes through the Strait under threat of a 'forceful response,' and unsold Iranian barrels are accumulating in floating storage as most buyers — except China — shy away from sanctions exposure. A temporary US easing of Russian oil sanctions, aimed at taming earlier price spikes, drew European objections but added to the bearish supply narrative. CME OPEC Watch options now price a further OPEC cut at 77% probability, reflecting market concern that the group will be forced to defend prices.
drivers: Saudi exports surging through reopened Strait of Hormuz flood the market with supply, accelerating the one-month -28% collapse in WTI
US temporary easing of Russian oil sanctions adds incremental supply and riles European allies, compounding bearish sentiment
Iran-related risk remains two-sided: floating storage of unsold barrels builds bearishly, but Tehran's 'forceful response' threat to tankers injects a residual geopolitical floor

gas.summary: Henry Hub slipped to $3.172/MMBtu (-1.49% on the day, -5.12% on the week) as domestic fundamentals remained soft, keeping the one-month change essentially flat at +0.16%. In contrast, European TTF surged to €43.995/MWh (+2.84% on the day, +8.89% on the week), driven by supply-security anxiety. Ukraine struck a Russian gas plant and Zelensky vowed further attacks; separately, Ukrainian drone strikes have triggered a severe fuel shortage inside Russia whose ripple effects are already reaching Central Asian importers — Kyrgyzstan, which sources over 90% of its gasoline from Russia, is scrambling for alternative supply. LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz have continued despite tensions, providing some offset, but the European market is clearly pricing escalating Russian supply risk more aggressively than the US domestic market.
drivers: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian gas infrastructure push TTF sharply higher on European supply-security concerns
Russian fuel crisis spills into Central Asia, with Kyrgyzstan seeking emergency alternatives as seasonal demand rises
Henry Hub softness persists; US domestic market decoupled from European tightness with one-month change near flat

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs held broadly steady at $75.55/EUA (+0.26% on the day), with the one-month trend modestly positive at +1.53%, even as TTF's sharp weekly rally of +8.89% raises generation-cost pressure on gas-fired power. The key policy headline was the EU conceding to Big Tech pressure and dropping its ten-year renewables rule for data centers, a move that could slow the pace of clean-energy offtake contracting. Offsetting that, Wall Street's pivot toward solar-plus-storage and an AI-driven record surge in battery demand signal robust long-run investment appetite for low-carbon capacity. Japanese banks committing $496 million to India's grid expansion underscores growing cross-border infrastructure financing. US-Iran Doha talks in Qatar focused on the Strait of Hormuz remain a background risk for LNG and power fuel supply chains.
drivers: EU drops ten-year renewables obligation for data centers under Big Tech lobbying, potentially softening near-term clean power demand signals
TTF's +8.89% weekly rally increases gas-fired generation costs and could support carbon prices if coal-to-gas switching reverses
AI-driven battery demand surge and Wall Street shift to solar-plus-storage point to accelerating clean power investment despite policy headwinds
